title: Patel Brothers, Big Lots, and the Quiet Conquest: Indian Grocery Stores Are Filling America's Empty Retail Spaces
excerpt: As legacy retailers shutter locations from Florida to Ohio, the nation's largest Indian grocery chain and its competitors are moving in — reshaping suburban food infrastructure one aisle at a time.
body:
There is a particular kind of excitement that only NRIs understand: the moment you discover that a Patel Brothers is opening near your suburb. It means fresh curry leaves on demand. It means proper atta flour, not the sad bag from the international aisle. It means the weekend grocery run no longer requires a 45-minute drive to the nearest desi enclave.

That excitement is spreading to more zip codes than ever. Patel Brothers, the largest Indian grocery chain in the United States, is in the middle of its most aggressive expansion in decades. At the same time, smaller competitors like India Grocers are seizing opportunities in markets the big chains have not yet reached. Together, they are quietly reshaping America's suburban retail landscape — often by moving into the very spaces that legacy American retailers abandoned.

## Filling the Gaps Legacy Retail Left Behind

In Dublin, Ohio, a suburb of Columbus, India Grocers is renovating a former Big Lots location at 6569 Sawmill Road. The discount retailer shuttered stores across Central Ohio in 2025, leaving vacant boxes that have become magnets for international grocery concepts catering to the region's fast-growing South Asian population.

The pattern is not unique to Ohio. Across the Sun Belt and in fast-growing suburban corridors, Indian grocery stores are taking over retail spaces vacated by chains that could not adapt to changing consumer habits. What was once a Big Lots or a Winn-Dixie is becoming a source of basmati rice in 25-kilogram bags and freshly made samosas from a steam table near the entrance.

## Patel Brothers: 50 Years and Counting

Patel Brothers was founded in 1974 in Chicago by two brothers who saw an opportunity to serve a community that mainstream grocers ignored. Five decades later, the company operates more than 50 stores across the country and remains the undisputed market leader in Indian grocery retail.

The chain's latest expansion is focused on Florida, where it is building a 20,000-square-foot store in St. Johns County — its second location in Northeast Florida. The new store, at the developing Shops at Racetrack Road, will include Patel's Fresh Kitchen, a bakery serving breads, samosas, and prepared foods, plus additional concepts including a restaurant, a jewelry store, and a beauty store.

"This has been something the community has been wanting and asking for, so it was great that this location came open," Swetal Patel, who heads day-to-day operations, told What Now. "We're looking forward to expanding our footprint in the Florida market." The company has three additional Florida locations in development, though details remain under wraps.

In Nashville, a new 25,000-square-foot Patel Brothers recently opened — the tenth location built by Knoebel Construction for the chain across eight states. The store features the full range of South Asian groceries, from dry goods and frozen items to fresh produce, along with the custom interior finishes that have become a signature of the brand's newer locations.

## More Than a Grocery Store

What makes the Patel Brothers model distinctive is its ambition to be more than a place to buy groceries. The newer locations function as community hubs — part grocery store, part food hall, part cultural anchor. Some stores, like those in McKinney, Texas, and Naperville, Illinois, even park green-and-yellow auto rickshaws outside the entrance, a touch that is equal parts marketing and nostalgia.

The prepared food counters, which offer everything from hot jalebis to fresh paneer, serve a dual purpose: they introduce non-Indian shoppers to South Asian cuisine while giving homesick NRIs a taste of the chaat stalls they grew up with. The in-store bakeries, now standard in new locations, produce naan, roti, and Indian sweets that rival dedicated sweet shops.

## The $15 Billion Backdrop

The expansion is not happening in a vacuum. The Indian food market in America is now worth an estimated $15 billion, according to industry analyses published this month. The US imported $711 million worth of Indian spices in the 2024-25 fiscal year, up 15 percent from the previous year. With 5.1 million Indians in the country — the second-largest Asian American community — and household incomes more than double the national average, the commercial case for Indian grocery retail has never been stronger.

Gen Z Americans are also discovering Indian cuisine beyond tikka masala. Biryani, chaat, dosa, and South Indian formats are building genuine consumer familiarity across urban markets nationwide. That mainstream curiosity is driving foot traffic to Indian grocery stores, where adventurous home cooks come seeking spice blends and specialty ingredients that no Whole Foods can stock in sufficient depth.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For NRIs, a new Patel Brothers in the neighborhood is more than a convenience — it is infrastructure. It means your kid's school potluck contribution no longer requires a heroic effort to source ingredients. It means Diwali prep does not start with a desperate online order from three states away. It means the ecosystem that supports daily Indian cooking — fresh methi, kadhi patta, green chillies that actually have heat — is finally catching up with where the diaspora actually lives.

The empty Big Lots on your commute may soon smell like cardamom and fresh naan. For 5.1 million Indian Americans, that is the most exciting retail development of the year.
